The rule table · Severity · Finding · Why it matters · · hard · RDM (raw device mapping) disk · no direct Proxmox equivalent — that storage needs a redesign · · hard · end-of-life Windows guest (XP/2003/2000/NT) · virtio drivers unavailable; legacy-device workarounds only · · moderate · snapshots present · chains don't convert — consolidate before export · · moderate · modern Windows guest · virtio drivers must go in before/at cutover · · minor · non-virtio NIC on Linux · model changes to virtio; the driver is already in-kernel · · minor · EFI firmware · recreate as OVMF VM, check Secure Boot expectations · · minor · > 2 TiB total disk · plan the transfer window · · minor · virtual hardware older than vmx-10 · verify ancient-guest assumptions · · info · powered on · schedule downtime or a re-sync cutover · · info · thick-provisioned disks · they export at full size · Verdict = the worst finding (info/minor → EASY). The rules are one readable function — extend them where your estate needs it. Usage bash ./vm-migration-assess.py --in inventory.json # human report ../vsphere-inventory/vsphere-inventory.py … · ./vm-migration-assess.py # piped ./vm-migration-assess.py --in inventory.json --json # machine-readable Exit codes · Code · Meaning · · 0 · assessed; no HARD VMs · · 1 · assessed; at least one HARD VM (both humans and pipelines branch on this) · · 2 · input isn't a readable inventory document · Tested on macOS 26 (Python 3.14) and Ubuntu 24.04 container (Python 3.12): live chain against vcsim (snapshot VM correctly MODERATE) plus a crafted fixture that fires every rule (RDM→HARD, XP→HARD, Windows 2022 + EFI + 3 TiB + snapshots → MODERATE, clean Linux → EASY with zero findings). The rule weights encode judgment, not measurements — lab-verified, and deliberately conservative.

toolbox/vsphere-inventory/README.md.b: vsphere-inventory > Inputs: --server host[:port] , --user , password via VSPHERE_PASSWORD · > Outputs: one JSON inventory document (stdout or --out ), optional per-VM > CSV · Risk: read-only — logs in, reads properties, logs out; changes > nothing · Root: not needed (a read-only vSphere role is enough) Inventory a vSphere environment with nothing but Python's standard library — no pyvmomi, no SDK, no govc. The tool speaks the vim25 SOAP API directly (XML over HTTPS via urllib ): it is both a working migration-assessment input and a demonstration that "the vCenter API" is just XML you can read. Collects per VM: power state, vCPU/memory, guest OS, firmware (BIOS/EFI), virtual hardware version, every disk (capacity, thin/thick, VMDK vs RDM ), every NIC (model, network, MAC), and the snapshot count — exactly the facts vm-migration-assess scores. Plus hosts, datastores, and networks. The JSON schema is shared with pve-inventory , so source and destination of a VMware→Proxmox move compare field by field. Usage bash export VSPHERE_PASSWORD='…' # keeps the secret off argv ./vsphere-inventory.py --server vcenter.lab --user readonly@vsphere.local \ --out inventory.json --csv vms.csv ./vsphere-inventory.py --server 127.0.0.1:8989 --user user --insecure # lab/vcsim --insecure skips TLS verification for self-signed lab vCenters. A dedicated read-only vSphere role is the right credential — the tool only ever reads. Prefer a maintained CLI for daily interactive work? govc does all of this and more. This tool exists where a zero-dependency, auditable, single-file collector is worth having (jump hosts, agents, teaching). Exit codes · Code · Meaning · · 0 · inventory written · · 1 · cannot reach the endpoint, or vCenter returned a fault (bad credentials, …) · · 2 · usage: no password provided · Tested on macOS 26 (Python 3.14) and Ubuntu 24.04 container (Python 3.12) against vcsim (govmomi's official vCenter simulator, 4 VMs/4 hosts): full document verified including snapshot counting (chained snapshots) and disk/NIC device parsing; connection-refused and missing-password paths exercised. vSphere 🔨 depth is real (VCP-level, production years); a run against a real vCenter is still pending — treat output-shape details against production vCenter versions as lab-verified, not production-proven.

h: What is drawn from the sheet, and what is not
Godot proves the floor; it does not draw it
tools/floor/README.md.b: tools/floor — the floor's design-time side > 🌐 Languages: English (default) · 中文 > Inputs: tiles.tiles , one character per pixel · Outputs: > site/assets/floor/tiles.png and tiles.json · Risk: writes two generated files > and nothing else · Root: not needed Everything here runs before the browser and never reaches it. The floor's runtime is site/js/floor.js , hand-written Canvas2D with no framework and no build step, exactly like the rest of the viewer (ADR-0006). bash python3 tools/floor/build-tiles.py # write the sheet and its index python3 tools/floor/build-tiles.py --check # exit non-zero when they are behind The tile source tiles.tiles is a palette followed by one sixteen-by-sixteen block per tile, drawn one character per pixel. It is the source; the PNG is derived and must never be hand-edited. The builder is deliberately rigid. A row that is not exactly sixteen characters, or a character the palette does not define, is a drawing mistake and it fails rather than padding — which it earned on its first run, catching a seventeen-character row that would otherwise have shifted a tile by a pixel and been noticed by nobody. Text in, raster out, on purpose. A tile change stays a reviewable diff, and the runtime still gets a sheet it can blit a few thousand times a frame without rasterising anything per load. That is the same trade ADR-0007 made for the hero figures. One palette, and it does not follow the reader's theme. A game scene has its own light, and honouring the theme toggle would mean two hand-drawn sheets plus a guard nobody has written (ADR-0013). Three rules decide what goes in it, and the first version of this sheet broke all three: Ramps are hue-shifted, never just darkened. Wood goes red into shadow and yellow into light; the monitor shell goes blue into shadow. A ramp built by dropping the brightness of one hue reads as plastic. Value is tiered by layer, and the floor is the darkest large area. Carpet sits lowest, furniture in the middle, the cast highest in local contrast, so a person reads against a desk and a desk reads against the carpet. The first sheet had a mid-light carpet, near-white walls and wood brighter than either — everything fought and the walls won. Tiles are designed edge-first. A wall is a band inside the cell, not the cell. Filling the cell made a partition read four tiles thick where two rooms met, because each room drew its own perimeter; the band lets two rooms share one visible wall. The projection is 45 degrees — front plus a little top-down, not isometric. You see the front of a monitor and the front of a drawer. Anything drawn pure top-down (the first chair was) sits at odds with everything around it. What is drawn from the sheet, and what is not · From tiles.tiles · Drawn in code · · Carpet, walls, windows, doors, desks, chairs, meeting tables, booths, racks, plants, printers, cabinets, the lobby's furniture · Which cell each of them lands in · · · The cast , generated from a small set of parts, because sixty-five figures need variation nobody is going to draw sixty-five times · · · Access points, segment swatches, coverage gradients, the legends · A pod is a bench. Two desk rows butted together with people on the outside, facing each other across a spine of monitors — which is what an open-plan floor is. The first version alternated a row of desks with a row of people, which is not a layout any office has. It is why there are two desk tiles and two chair tiles: the far side of the bench shows the backs of its monitors, and a chair's back is on the side the sitter is not facing. Every sprite call has a flat fallback. If the sheet fails to load, the floor still draws and the argument still stands — a missing decoration should not take the material down with it. Godot proves the floor; it does not draw it ADR-0013 settles that Godot is design-time and never ships to the browser. That still holds. What changed is what it is for . bash python3 tools/floor/prove-topology.py # walk the floor, report python3 tools/floor/prove-topology.py --stamp # walk it, then record the verdict python3 tools/floor/prove-topology.py --check # for CI: is the plate still proved? The plate is hand-authored JSON and stays that way. Generating a layout in headless GDScript is only writing the same coordinates in a language that reviews worse — the exact objection ADR-0013 raised against .tscn . What Godot does instead is the thing that cannot be asserted: It walks the floor. godot/prove_topology.gd floods from the lift lobby along circulation only and reports any room or space it cannot reach, and any desk cell it would have to cross. On its first run it failed, and it was right to: the lobby's door opened at x=5 while the corridor ring began at x=8, and the large room's door opened at x=40 while the ring ended at x=37. Two doors opening onto nothing, in a plan that looked fine. Neither would have survived the proof and neither was going to be caught by eye. --stamp records the date, the verdict and a fingerprint of the plate's geometry — the rectangles, the doors, the circulation, the pods, and nothing else, so renaming a room does not invalidate a proof while moving a wall does. --check compares that fingerprint, which is why a clone without Godot is not stuck : it skips the walk, still catches a plate that has moved since anyone proved it, and exits 0. The promise that a reader installs nothing is a promise to the reader; a contributor moving a wall installs Godot. What it does not check, deliberately: corridor widths, egress distances, travel distance to an exit, sanitary provision. Those are architecture, and ADR-0014 is where the line is argued.

walkthrough/01-the-network.en.md.t: Walkthrough 01 · The network — one floor, four segments, and the radios in the ceiling
walkthrough/01-the-network.en.md.b: Walkthrough 01 · The network — one floor, four segments, and the radios in the ceiling The lift doors open onto an empty floor. No partitions, no carpet, the ceiling still hanging half-finished with the cable tray showing above it. There are some chalk marks on the slab from whoever looked at it last. The windows are big. The light is good. That is all there is. The agent standing in the doorway says it seats a hundred people. A hundred is a payroll number. It is not a number about this room. Those two have never been the same number, and almost every design that goes wrong starts by treating them as one. Put enough buildings side by side and a very steady curve shows up. On the busiest midweek day, attendance runs in the mid sixties percent. Which means a hundred-person office, on a Tuesday, is a sixty-five-person office. Monday is low fifties. Friday is high thirties. Same floor, same people, same week. So you size for Tuesday. Not for the payroll, and not for Friday. Size for a hundred and what you have bought is a space that sits half empty every day of the year, and you will pay rent on it for ten of them. Size for Friday and Tuesday does not fit. And not fitting is something that happens once a week, every week, not occasionally. Desks first. A desk per person stopped being the rule some time ago; hybrid offices provision somewhere between six and eight desks for every ten people. Take seven, and a hundred people means seventy desks. That seats a sixty-five-person peak comfortably and leaves a little room for the day it runs over. Meeting rooms scale at roughly one per ten to twenty people. Where you land inside that range is not decided by headcount, it is decided by how open the floor is. A fully open floor pushes toward one per ten, because people with no door need somewhere to go. This floor is open. So, seven. How you split those seven is where most offices get it wrong, and this one has actually been measured. Sensors across thirteen countries, a hundred and seventy-three buildings and more than twenty-seven thousand workspaces found that eight in ten meetings happen in rooms built for six or fewer. And the big room, the one that seats seventeen or more, sits at twelve percent utilisation. Four days out of five, it is a locked empty room. So: one large, two medium, four small. Roughly half the rooms seat two to four people. Then six phone booths on top of that. They are not small meeting rooms. They solve a different problem — one person needs to take a call — and folding them into the meeting room count is the standard way a floor ends up with nowhere to take a call. Good. People, desks, rooms. All of them have numbers now. The network is next. The instinct at this point is to ask what to buy. Whose switches, how many access points, which firewall. I would leave that question alone for a while, because it is the fifth question, not the first. Strip every vendor away and a site network answers four things. And they come in an order. One. Who is allowed to talk to whom. That is segmentation. Two. What the addresses are, and what they will collide with. That is the address plan. Three. How things get on. Wired ports, wireless, and what authenticates them. Four. Who answers a name and who hands out a lease. Which is to say, who owns DNS and DHCP. The order is not for tidiness. Each one constrains the next. You cannot write an address plan until you know what needs separating, and you cannot say where something lands until you know what the addresses look like. Get the order wrong and you get a very familiar result. The floor is addressed and cabled before anyone decides what should be separated. Segmentation becomes a retrofit. And a retrofit is the kind of work that goes on a plan and never comes off it. Segmentation first, and there is one rule. A segment per trust level, never a segment per device type. The first is staff. That is the default one — authenticated humans and the managed devices in their hands. The second is guest. Untrusted people, internet only, and the isolation has to be provable rather than assumed. The third one I tend to call the unpatchable. Door controllers, printers, the appliance in the meeting room, whatever is sitting on the lab bench. What they have in common is not that they are hardware. It is that they run vendor firmware, on a vendor's schedule, and they sit where anybody can walk up and reach them. Those three things together are why they get their own segment. The fourth is management. The management interfaces on the switches and the access points, reachable from exactly one place. Four is usually right. Five is usually a mistake. Because every extra segment is another rule set, and somebody has to stand up a year from now and explain why it looks the way it does. That somebody may not be you. The extra segments almost always arrive carrying the word tidy. One per department. One per floor. One per kind of thing. And a tidy split produces exactly the rules that nobody can defend on the day they break something. So the test for a proposed segment is not, are these things different. The test is, what am I willing to block between them, and will I actually block it. A segment with an any-to-any rule back to the staff network is a VLAN, not a security boundary. Calling it a boundary is how an estate acquires a control that exists only on the diagram. The address plan. This gets written before the first subnet exists. And it gets written against the thing that will one day break it, which is: somewhere you will eventually have to tunnel to. Every site, every branch, every VPN pool, every network in every cloud. None of them overlapping. Not probably fine. Checked. And one more. Do not pick 192.168.0.0 or 192.168.1.0. They work perfectly, right up until the day you need to reach them from somewhere that also chose them. Every home router and half the vendor appliances in the world ship defaulted into that space. Size it for the growth in the lease, not for move-in day. This floor grows to about a hundred and thirty people without anyone moving. An address plan that fits exactly a hundred is a renumbering that has already been scheduled. Nobody has picked the date yet. And leave gaps on purpose. Contiguous allocation looks tidy, and it makes the next segment impossible to summarise. Allocate as though a summary route will one day matter, because on the day you add a second site, it does. Here is what that rule is actually protecting you from. Two companies merge, or two estates have to reach each other, and both of them years ago picked out of the ten-dot space. From there you have three options. Renumber one side. NAT the overlap. Or proxy the whole thing at the application layer. None of the three is an afternoon's work. All three are projects with names, budgets, and somebody assigned to them. Which is why the word checked earns the two hours it costs on day one. Third question. How things get on. Wireless is the access layer now. That did not make wired go away. It changed what wired is for. The first thing that still wants a cable is the access point itself. And this is the requirement that actually decides which switch you buy. Not the desk port count. Those few access point ports. A current access point wants a higher tier of power over ethernet and a two-and-a-half gigabit uplink. The second is the screens and the room systems. A device carrying a meeting should not be competing for airtime, in that room, with every phone belonging to the people in the meeting. The third is printers, door controllers, everything sitting on that unpatchable segment. A cable is also a placement decision, and a wired port is far easier to pin to a VLAN than a wireless client is. The fourth is desks. Still. But not because people use them. Most people will never plug in. The reason is that pulling cable during a fit-out costs a rounding error, and pulling it afterwards is a project that lifts ceilings, clears floors, and needs a written method. Generous drops are cheap now and expensive later. Somewhere around here somebody asks: is it still gigabit? That question has three answers, because there are three tiers in this building and they move at different times, for different reasons. The desk port has almost nothing pushing on it. Hybrid moved the load to wireless and the storage to SaaS. The desk is the least starved link in the building. Upgrading it first is the classic misread, and the most common way to spend the budget in the wrong ceiling. The tier that actually moves is the access point uplink. A current access point can exceed a gigabit on its radios alone. Give it a gigabit port and you have turned that access point into the bottleneck it was bought to remove. Multi-gig earns its money here, and only here. The third tier is aggregation and core, and what matters there is oversubscription. Every access switch uplink lands here, and this is where a design quietly gets capped. The order matters more than the numbers. The instinct is to upgrade the tier people can see, and the tier people can see is the one that needs it least. Uplink and stacking are where the under-specification lives, for a simple reason. Access port count is easy to count, so it is rarely wrong. The path from access to core appears on no port list at all, so nobody counts it. Fourth question, and the shortest one. Who answers a name, and who hands out a lease. DNS and DHCP are not technically hard. What is hard is ownership. Who is responsible, and who gets woken up. That has never been a technical question, and it will arrive in your ticket queue dressed as one. And authentication. Authentication on a port is identity wearing a networking hat. It belongs to the identity story; it just turns up wearing the network's clothes. Let me name a few things here, so that you can recognise where you are when you walk into an unfamiliar comms room. The thing doing the authenticating on the port is 802.1X. Standing behind it, answering who is this, is usually RADIUS. And behind RADIUS sits your directory. LLDP is how switches announce themselves to each other. A DHCP relay is what carries a request across a segment to a server that is not on it. How any of them completes a handshake, what the frames look like — I am not going to cover. Not because it does not matter. Because it is a different ability. Recognising where you are standing, and being able to say what the wire is doing at this instant, can be learned separately, and this walk only teaches the first one. And back to the guest network one last time. The isolation has to be provable. Clients isolated from each other, outbound only, and you should be able to demonstrate it, not point at it on a diagram. Right. Look up. The ceiling. Before I talk about radios, I want to change my footing. Everything so far — segments, addresses, who authenticates, which tier moves — is work I have actually done and then lived with for years afterwards. The wireless arithmetic coming next is not. It is read, cross-checked and worked through, out of published vendor engineering guidance, and I have checked it for internal consistency. But I have not designed an office wireless deployment and then lived with it for three years. Those two things do not weigh the same, so I would rather say it than let a confident tone paper over it. The method itself is solid, and solid enough that it has barely moved across several generations of radio. Count it twice, take the larger, then check it against coverage. First count. By client. Sixty-five people on the floor on a Tuesday, at roughly two devices each. Add seven room systems, the devices in six booths, a few printers, a few door controllers. About a hundred and forty-five associated devices. An access point in a dense space handles a hundred clients on paper, but you plan around twenty-five active per radio and about fifty per access point. That is an airtime fairness limit rather than a spec sheet one, which is exactly why it has barely moved in a decade. A hundred and forty-five over fifty is about three. Second count. By throughput. Per client targets: video conferencing around one and a half megabits, high definition video around three, a voice call small enough to ignore. Size on the highest bitrate application, not the average one. About forty percent of devices are active at peak. Fifty-eight devices at three megabits is around a hundred and seventy-four megabits. One access point covers that. Three and one. Take the larger. Three. Now check it against coverage. A partitioned office wants roughly one access point per two and a half to three thousand square feet. This floor is about eleven thousand. That gives four. Notice what just happened. What binds the number is coverage, not capacity. That surprises people, because everything they have been told says density is what matters now. Density does decide it — above about a hundred and fifty people. Below that, the coverage floor usually wins. Last step. Place them for the busiest square metre, not the average one. Uniform spacing serves a floor with meeting rooms in it worse than deliberate placement does. And the large room earns a radio of its own. It is the only square metre on this floor where twenty cameras come on at the same moment, and at that moment there are not twenty people in the corridor outside it. Add that in and you land on five or six. So at this size, density decides where they go and coverage decides how many there are. Those two get collapsed into one sentence constantly, and once collapsed the sentence is no longer usable. Last stop. Down to the rack. Count the ports. Seventy desks. Seven rooms with a display and a room system each, fourteen. Six booths. Six access points. Three or so printers. Three or so door controllers and readers. Then eight for signage, spares, and the things nobody has thought of yet. About a hundred and ten active ports. With growth to a hundred and thirty people, about a hundred and thirty-five. Three forty-eight port switches. But the thing that actually picks which switch is usually not the port count. It is the power budget. Six access points, plus the room and booth devices, plus door access, lands near five hundred watts of simultaneous draw. And two switches with the same forty-eight ports can differ by more than a factor of two on power budget. Same port count, completely different set of things they can actually carry. So specify the watts. Not just the ports. And uplink and stacking. That is the second time today, because it is the one thing in all of this that is both load-bearing and will never raise its hand to remind you it exists. Look back at what bound each answer. The desk count was bound by Tuesday. The room mix was bound by those eight-in-ten meetings of six people or fewer. The radio count was bound by coverage, not capacity. The switch was bound by watts, not ports. Not one of those four is the intuitive answer. So next time you are standing in an empty floor plate, you can leave the buying question alone for a while. Ask who is allowed to talk to whom. Everything else lines up behind that one.

walkthrough/01-the-network.zh.md.t: 走读 01 · 网络——一层楼、四个网段，和天花板上的那几个天线
walkthrough/01-the-network.zh.md.b: 走读 01 · 网络——一层楼、四个网段，和天花板上的那几个天线 电梯门开的时候，这层楼是空的。没有隔断，没有地毯，天花板还吊在半空，露出上面一格一格的桥架。地上有几处白色的粉笔线，是上一拨看房的人留下的。窗户很大，光很好。就这样。 中介站在门口说，这里能坐一百个人。 一百这个数字，是工资单上的数字，不是这个房间里的数字。这两个数字从来不一样，而所有做错的设计，几乎都是从把它们当成同一个开始的。 把很多栋楼的实际人数放在一起看，会看到一条很稳定的曲线。周中最忙的那天，到场率在百分之六十五上下。也就是说，一间一百人的办公室，星期二的时候，是一间六十五个人的办公室。 星期一是五十出头。星期五是三十几。同一层楼，同一批人，同一个星期。 所以你按星期二来定尺寸。不按工资单，也不按星期五。 按一百来定，你买下的是一片一年三百六十五天都有一半空着的地方，而且你会为它付十年租金。 按星期五来定，星期二就装不下。而装不下这件事，是每周都会发生一次的，不是偶尔。 桌子先定下来。现在的办公室，桌子早就不是一人一张了，混合办公之下大概是零点六到零点八张。取零点七，一百个人就是七十张桌子。它舒服地坐得下六十五个人，还留了点余地给偶尔超出的那天。 会议室按人头算，大概每十到二十个人一间。落在这个区间的哪一头，不看人数，看这层楼开不开放。全开放的楼面往十那头走，因为没有门的人总得有地方可去。这层楼是开放的，所以是七间。 七间的分法，是大多数办公室真正做错的地方，而且这件事是被量过的。有人在十三个国家、一百七十三栋楼、两万七千多个工位上装了传感器，结果是：八成的会议发生在六个人以内的房间里。 而那种能坐十七个人以上的大会议室，利用率是百分之十二。它一年里有八成的时间，是一间上了锁的空房子。 所以是一间大的，两间中的，四间小的。差不多一半的房间只坐两到四个人。 另外还要六个电话亭。它们不是小号的会议室，它们解决的是另一件事——一个人要打个电话。把电话亭算进会议室的数量里，是一层楼最后变成没地方接电话的标准做法。 好。人、桌子、房间，都有数了。现在轮到网络。 第一反应通常是问买什么。买哪家的交换机，买几个 AP，防火墙用谁的。我建议先把这个问题放一放，因为它是第五个问题，不是第一个。 一个场地的网络，剥掉所有厂商之后，只回答四件事。而且这四件事有顺序。 第一，谁被允许跟谁说话。这是分段。 第二，地址是什么，它会跟什么撞上。这是地址规划。 第三，东西怎么接进来。有线口、无线、以及谁来认证它们。 第四，谁回答一个名字，谁发一个租约。也就是 DNS 和 DHCP 归谁管。 顺序不是我排着好看的。每一个都在约束下一个。你不知道要隔开什么，就没法定地址；你不知道地址长什么样，就没法说谁接进来落在哪。 把顺序搞反，会得到一个非常经典的结果：楼面已经编好址、线也拉完了，才有人开始想应该隔开什么。于是分段变成一次改造。而改造这种事，是排进计划、然后永远不会做的那一类。 先说分段。一条规矩：按信任级别分，不按设备类型分。 第一个网段是员工。这是默认的那个——认证过的人，和他们手上被管理的设备。 第二个是访客。不被信任的人，只给上网，而且隔离要能被证明，不是"应该是隔开的"。 第三个，我习惯叫它"打不了补丁的那些"。门禁控制器、打印机、会议室里的一体机、实验台上的设备。 它们的共同点不是"都是硬件"，而是：跑着厂商的固件，按厂商的时间表更新，而且就摆在任何人都能走过去伸手够到的地方。这三条加在一起，才是它们该被单独隔出来的理由。 第四个是管理网。交换机和 AP 的管理口，只能从一个地方够得着。 四个，通常是对的。 五个，通常是错的。 因为每多一个网段，就是多一套规则，而这套规则一年之后要有人站出来解释它为什么长这样。那个人可能不是你。 最常见的多余网段，都来自"整齐"这个理由。一个部门一个，一层楼一个，一种设备一个。整齐的分法，产出的正好是那种在出问题的时候没人能替它辩护的规则。 所以判断一个网段该不该存在，问题不是"这些东西不一样吗"。问题是：我打算在它们之间挡掉什么，以及——我真的会去挡吗。 一个对员工网开着任意到任意的网段，是一个 VLAN，不是一道安全边界。把它叫成边界，是一套环境获得那种只存在于图纸上的控制措施的标准方式。 地址规划。这件事要在第一个子网存在之前写完。 而且写的时候，要对着那个将来会把它撞坏的东西写。那个东西是：某个你有一天要打隧道过去的地方。 每一个站点、每一个分支、每一个 VPN 地址池、每一朵云里的每一个网络，互相都不能重叠。 不是"应该不会重"。是核对过。 还有一条：不要选 192.168.0.0 和 192.168.1.0 这两段。 它们用起来完全没问题，一直到某一天，你要从一个也选了同样地址的地方访问它。而每一台家用路由器、以及一半的厂商设备，出厂默认就落在那两段里。 容量按租约里的增长算，不按搬进来那天算。这层楼不搬家的话，大概会长到一百三十个人。 一个刚好装得下一百人的地址规划，是一次已经安排好、只是还没定日期的重新编址。 还有，故意留空。连续分配看起来很整齐，但它会让下一个网段没办法被汇总进来。 分配的时候就当作有一天汇总路由会重要，因为在你加第二个站点的那天，它就重要了。 说说这条规矩防的到底是什么。两家公司合并，或者两个环境要互通，而两边当初都用了 10 打头的那一大块地址。 到这一步只有三条路：一边重新编址，或者给重叠的部分做 NAT，或者干脆在应用层做代理。 三条路都不是一个下午能做完的活。三条路都是有名字、有预算、有人被指派去负责的项目。这就是为什么那句"核对过"值得在第一天多花的那两个小时。 第三个问题：东西怎么接进来。 现在的接入层是无线。这件事没有让有线消失，它改变的是有线用来干什么。 第一样还需要线的，是 AP 本身。 而且这一条才是真正决定你买什么交换机的需求——不是桌面的端口数，是 AP 那几个口。现在的 AP 要更高一档的以太网供电，还要一个二点五千兆的上行口。 第二样是会议室的屏幕和一体机。一台正在承载会议的设备，不该在它自己承载的那间会议里，跟屋里所有人的手机抢空口。 第三样是打印机、门禁，以及所有落在"打不了补丁"那个网段里的东西。一根线同时也是一个位置决定，而且一个有线口比一个无线客户端更容易被牢牢按在某个 VLAN 上。 第四样，桌子还是要拉线。 但理由不是因为大家会用。大部分人不会插那根线。 理由是：装修的时候拉线，成本是个零头；装修完了再拉，是一个要动天花板、要清场、要写方案的项目。慷慨一点的点位，现在很便宜，以后很贵。 接下来会有人问一句：现在还是千兆吗。 这句话有三个答案，因为楼里有三个档位，它们在不同的时间、因为不同的理由升级。 桌面口，几乎什么都没推着它动。混合办公把负载搬去了无线，把存储搬去了 SaaS。桌面那一段，是整栋楼里最不饿的一段。 先升级桌面口，是最经典的一次误读，也是把预算花在错误的那片天花板上的最常见方式。 真正在动的是 AP 的上行口。 一个现在的 AP，光是它的射频就能超过一个千兆。你给它一个千兆的口，就是把这个 AP 变成了它本来被买来消除的那个瓶颈。多千兆在这里赚到钱，只在这里。 第三档是汇聚和核心。这里看的是收敛比。每一台接入交换机的上联都落在这，而一个设计通常就是在这里被悄悄封顶的。 顺序比数字重要。直觉是先升级人看得见的那一段，而人看得见的那一段恰好是最不需要的那一段。 上联和堆叠是最容易被欠配的地方，原因很简单：接入层的端口数很好数，所以很少数错；而从接入到核心的那条路径，不出现在任何一张端口清单上，所以没有人去数它。 第四个问题，也是最短的一个：谁回答一个名字，谁发一个租约。 DNS 和 DHCP 在技术上都不难。难的是所有权——谁负责它，谁在半夜被叫醒。这从来不是一个技术问题，它是一个组织问题，而它会以技术问题的样子出现在你的工单里。 还有认证。端口上的认证，其实是身份戴了一顶网络的帽子。它属于身份那条线，只是穿了网络的衣服出现。 这里我点几个名字，是为了让你走进一个陌生的机房时认得出来自己在哪。 端口上做认证的，是 802.1X。站在它后面回答"这个人是谁"的，通常是 RADIUS，而 RADIUS 背后连的是你的目录。 交换机之间互相报家门的，是 LLDP。跨网段把 DHCP 请求转过去的，是 DHCP 中继。 它们怎么握手、报文长什么样，我不打算讲。 不是因为它不重要，是因为它是另一种能力。认得出你身在何处，和说得出线上此刻正在发生什么，这两件事可以分开学，而今天这一趟只教前一件。 最后回到访客网。访客隔离要做到可证明——客户端之间互相隔离，只出不进，而且这件事你要能演示给别人看，不是能在图上指给别人看。 好，抬头。天花板。 在讲天线之前，我要换一个说法。 上面这些——分段、地址、谁认证、哪一档该升级——是我真的做过、并且跟着它过了几年的东西。接下来这一段无线的算术，不是。它是查来的、对过的、算过的，来源是厂商公开的工程指南，我核对过它内部是不是自洽。但我没有设计完一套办公室无线、然后跟它一起生活三年。这两件事的分量不一样，所以我把它说出来，而不是让语气把它盖过去。 方法本身很稳，稳到跨了好几代射频都没怎么变：数两遍，取大的那个，然后再拿覆盖去卡一次。 第一遍，按客户端数。 星期二这层楼上有六十五个人，一人算两台设备。再加七套会议室系统、六个电话亭里的设备、几台打印机、几个门禁控制器。加起来大概一百四十五台关联设备。 一个 AP 在密集环境里，大概承一百个客户端是纸面数字，实际按每个射频二十五个、每台五十个来规划才是稳的——这是空口公平性的限制，不是规格书上的限制，所以它这么多年几乎没变过。一百四十五除以五十，大约三个。 第二遍，按吞吐。 每客户端的目标值：视频会议大概一点五兆，高清视频大概三兆，语音通话小到可以忽略。要按最高码率的那个应用来算，不是按平均。 峰值时段大概四成的设备是活跃的，五十八台乘三兆，大约一百七十四兆。一个 AP 就够了。 两遍的结果是三和一。取大的：三个。 然后拿覆盖来卡。一个有隔断的办公空间，大概每两千五到三千平方英尺要一个 AP。这层楼一万一千平方英尺左右。 除下来，四个。 注意发生了什么。绑住结果的不是容量，是覆盖。 这一点常常让人意外，因为大家听到的说法都是"现在是密度决定一切"。密度确实会决定一切——在一百五十个人以上。在这个规模以下，赢的通常是覆盖那条线。 最后一步，按最忙的那一平米摆，不是按平均。均匀布点这件事，对一层有会议室的楼面来说，是比刻意布点更差的做法。 那间大会议室，值一个专属的射频。因为它是这层楼上唯一一个会出现"二十个人同时开摄像头"的地方，而那一刻它周围的走廊上并没有二十个人。 把这个加进去，最终是五到六个。 所以在这个规模上，密度决定它们放在哪里，覆盖决定它们有几个。这两句话经常被混成一句，而混成一句之后就没法用了。 最后，我们下楼，走到机柜前面。 先数端口。七十个桌面口。七间会议室，每间一个屏幕加一台一体机，十四个。六个电话亭。六个 AP。三台左右打印机。三个左右门禁和读卡器。再给指示牌、备用、和现在还想不到的东西留八个。 加起来，大约一百一十个在用的口。 加上长到一百三十人的增长，大约一百三十五。三台四十八口的交换机。 但真正决定你买哪台的，往往不是口数。 是供电瓦数。六个 AP，加上会议室和电话亭里的设备，加上门禁，同时工作的时候大概在五百瓦上下。 而两台同样是四十八口的交换机，供电预算可以差一倍以上。口数一样，能带的东西完全不是一回事。 所以在需求里写瓦数，不要只写口数。 另外，上联和堆叠。这是今天第二次提它，因为它是这一整件事里唯一一个既重要、又不会自己冒出来提醒你的地方。 回头看一遍今天绑住每个结果的是什么。桌子的数量，是星期二绑的。会议室的分法，是六个人以内那八成会议绑的。天线的数量，是覆盖绑的，不是容量。交换机的型号，是瓦数绑的，不是口数。 这四条里，没有一条是那个最直觉的答案。 下次你站在一层空楼面前面，可以先不问买什么。先问谁能跟谁说话。剩下的东西，会顺着这个问题自己排好队。

walkthrough/02-the-first-monday.en.md.t: Walkthrough 02 · The first Monday — one joiner, and the two things nothing ever triggers
walkthrough/02-the-first-monday.en.md.b: Walkthrough 02 · The first Monday — one joiner, and the two things nothing ever triggers It is ten to nine on a Monday, and there is somebody standing in the lift lobby who has never been here before. The floor behind them is not the one from the first walk. The partitions are up, the ceiling is closed, the cable tray is out of sight where it belongs. Seventy desks, seven meeting rooms, six booths. Somebody is already making coffee. This person is not special. They are one of about twenty-three people who will do exactly this in the next twelve months. Four things have to be true before they can sit down and work. An account that says who they are. A machine. A way onto the network. And a seat on whatever this company uses to get anything done. None of those four gets built today. Every one of them had to be true before the lift doors opened. Monday does not build anything. Monday reveals what was built. That is the whole reason this walk is worth taking. So go back. Something, somewhere, decided that this person exists. What was it? If the answer is that a manager filed a ticket, stop. Everything downstream of that answer is going to be late, incomplete, or both, and no amount of automation further along will fix it. The question worth asking is narrower and much harder. What system decides whether a person is still an employee? There has to be one. Not two that mostly agree. One, named, that everything else believes. Usually it is whatever HR runs, because that is where the start date and the last day actually live. It is rarely the system anybody wants it to be, and it is almost never the directory. Given that trigger, the account is the easy half. A name, a mailbox, a password nobody has yet used. What they can reach is the hard half, and it is decided by one rule that sounds like pedantry until the second year. A group means a job function, or a group means an access bundle. Never both. Because the moment a group means both, it cannot be changed for one reason without changing the other. Move somebody between teams and their access moves with them, silently, in a direction nobody chose. And automation is faithful. It applies the model exactly as written. If the model confuses those two things, the automation propagates the confusion at machine speed, to every new hire, consistently. Consistent is worse than sporadic here. A sporadic mess gets noticed. A consistent one becomes the way things are done. This office has eight functions. Finance, sales, engineering, and five more. Eight is a small number. It is small enough that nobody thinks a group model is worth designing, and large enough that the wrong one takes years to unwind. Somewhere in the same week, a laptop was ordered. The interesting part is where its image lives, and the answer today is: not in this building. Nobody here builds it. The vendor registers the machine to this company before it ships, and on first boot it reaches out and pulls its own policy. That replaced a task-sequence server, a technician, and thirty to sixty minutes per machine. It only works if the identity work was done first. If it was not, this is not zero-touch. It is a re-imaging project wearing zero-touch as a costume. The box itself arrived on Thursday and went into the store, which is the room with a door that locks, sitting next to the rack. The store is not big. It holds about five spare machines, the returns that have not been wiped yet, and whatever is in transit. Five sounds thin until you work out what it is for. Five covers the joiners arriving before the next order lands, which is about two a month, and the machines that die in that same month, which is a fraction of one. It is a lead-time number, not a stock policy. And then the seats. This office can name about ten services it owns. A directory, a productivity tenant, file storage, device management, endpoint security, backup, remote access, a ticket system, conferencing, and something watching all of it. Our joiner also needs a seat on at least one thing that is not on that list, because somebody in their team bought it on a card eighteen months ago and never told anyone. Hold onto that one. It comes back at the end, and it is the most expensive sentence in this walk. Back to the lobby. Ten to nine. The walk from the lift to their desk goes past the service desk, and that is not an accident. It sits on the circulation route, visible from the floor, near the store it draws stock from and near the rack it is first responder for. Put that same position in a back office and something specific happens. The walk-ups become tickets. Nobody decided to change the workload. Somebody moved a desk. Their desk is one of seventy, in a floor built for sixty-five people on a Tuesday. There is a chair. There is a monitor. There is a machine that has never been switched on. First boot. It asks who they are. Note what it does not ask. It does not ask what the machine is, or where it is, or which cable it is attached to. It asks who is holding it. And when it reaches the network, the network asks the same question. That is 802.1X, and behind it RADIUS, and behind RADIUS the same directory that issued the account. The port does not decide anything. You could carry this machine to any desk on this floor, or into any of the seven meeting rooms, and it would land in the same place. Which is the staff segment, because they authenticated. There are four segments on this floor and that is the one for people who proved who they are. The other three are guest, unpatchable, and management. Guest is worth a sentence, because it is the only one with no register at all. You do not enrol a visitor. You size that segment by the peak day and let it be untrusted, and being untrusted on purpose is what makes it safe. By lunchtime our joiner is working. Mail, files, chat, the tool their team lives in. Nobody walked them through a setup wizard. So how many tickets did today generate? If all of it was built properly, close to none. Here is that number from two directions. The support model says enrolment and imaging generate about fifty-three tickets a year once zero-touch is built. The fleet arithmetic says the office hands over about sixty-two machines a year, counting refresh and joiners together. Seven tickets for every eight handovers. Most machines change hands and nobody files anything at all, and some do not, and that gap is what a working provisioning path looks like from the outside. Those two numbers were derived from completely different things. One from ticket rates, one from a refresh cycle. They describe the same office and they agree, which is the only kind of confirmation this sort of planning can offer. Now do all of that twenty-three times. And about seventeen times in the other direction, because people leave. This is where the footing under this walk changes, and it is worth saying out loud rather than letting it slide past. The turnover figure is borrowed. A rate in the middle teens is the band professional-services and technology employers usually sit in, and that band comes from published employer figures, not from anybody here having run this company's payroll. What is not borrowed is the structure. Joiners equal leavers plus growth. That sentence is arithmetic and it does not care what the turnover rate is. So move the band. Take it down to one in ten and every number after this changes. The shape of the argument does not move at all, and the shape is the part worth carrying to your own building. At the middle of that band it comes to about forty joiner-and-leaver events a year. One about every six working days. Not a project. Not a season. Every six working days, for as long as the lease runs. The lease runs five years. Across it this office hires about a hundred and sixteen people. In order to grow by thirty. Add the hundred who were already here on day one, and roughly two hundred and sixteen different people hold an account in this company at some point. For a floor that never holds more than a hundred and thirty of them at once. Which means the directory is not the office. It is about one and seven tenths of the office, and that ratio only grows. An office is a snapshot. A register is a history. Every estate IT administers is the second kind, and every intuition people have about size is the first kind. The machines do exactly the same thing. About two hundred and twenty bought across the lease, to hold about a hundred and fifteen at a time. Now go forward three years and find the person from Monday morning. They are still here. They changed teams eighteen months ago. Think about what each of the three lifecycle events actually gives you to work with. A joiner has a start date. A leaver has a last day. A mover has a conversation. No event fires. Nothing arrives in a queue. There is no date on which somebody is required to look, and so the move is handled the way conversations are handled, which is by granting what is now needed. And not removing what is not. Everybody builds it this way. It looks finished, because joiners work and leavers work. Two years and a few internal transfers later, the people who have been here longest have the most access in the company, and not one of them can tell you why. Nobody was careless. Every individual grant was correct on the day it was made. The failure is that the leg with no trigger never got one. That is one thing in this office that nothing ever triggers. Here is the other, and it is larger. Count the identities in this building that are not people. There are about forty. Twenty-six of them are device credentials, because the network authenticates everything and the door controllers, the printers, the room systems and the booth devices all have to answer for themselves. About a dozen are service integrations between the ten named services. Two are break-glass accounts. Two identities in every five in this office are not a person. Not one of the forty has a start date. Not one of them has a manager. And not one of them has a last day. Think about the door controller. A leaver forces a review of one person's access, because a date arrives and a process starts. Nothing at all forces a review of a door controller's credential. It was issued during the fit-out and it will still be there when the lease ends. The three privileged administrator accounts are the exception that proves the rule. They do expire, eventually, because the human behind each one eventually leaves. And now the sentence from earlier comes back. The tool somebody bought on a card. When our joiner eventually leaves, the leaver process will revoke their seats on the ten services this company can name. It will not touch that one, because no leaver event reaches a service nobody wrote down. That is not a reclamation rate that could be improved. It is not ninety percent, or eighty. There is no process there at all. Across one lease, eighty-six people leave this company. For anything outside the named ten, nobody revokes anything, because nobody with a revocation duty knows the tool exists. There is a place where all of this becomes visible, and it is the ticket queue. Build the automation the sixteen steps ask for. Self-service password reset, zero-touch devices, automated joiner-mover-leaver. It works. It removes about two fifths of the ticket volume. One category does not move at all. Access and permissions. Afterwards it is the largest thing left in the queue, more than a third of everything. That is not a gap in the automation. It is the estate arriving in the queue. Access requests are produced by an identity population that is two fifths non-human with no lifecycle, against a service estate whose size this company does not know, over a register that changes about a hundred and twenty-three times a year. Automating the request path does not shrink any of that. It just makes the same requests arrive faster. Look at which categories the sixteen steps do remove. Password resets. Enrolment. Joiner and leaver runs. Every one of them is a question with a deterministic answer. And the one that survives is the one that ends with a person deciding whether somebody should be allowed to have something. That is the same boundary every step of the build-out arrives at when it asks what AI can be trusted with. Next Monday there will be another one of these. Somebody in the lobby at ten to nine who has never been here before. This floor empties every Friday and fills again on Tuesday. Sixty-five people, a hundred and forty-five devices in the air, seventy desks, and by the high thirties on a Friday afternoon almost nobody. The estate does not empty. It has never once, in the life of this lease, been smaller than it was the day before. So when you are working out what a hundred-person office needs, count the people twice. Once for the desks, the radios and the rooms, which is what the building asks for. And once for everyone who has ever held an account, which is what you are actually administering.

walkthrough/02-the-first-monday.zh.md.t: 走读 02 · 第一个星期一——一个新人，和两件永远没人触发的事
walkthrough/02-the-first-monday.zh.md.b: 走读 02 · 第一个星期一——一个新人，和两件永远没人触发的事 星期一，八点五十。电梯厅里站着一个人，他没来过这里。 他身后那层楼，已经不是第一次走读里的那层了。隔断立起来了，天花板封上了，桥架回到了它该待的地方。七十张桌子，七间会议室，六个电话亭。有人已经在煮咖啡了。 这个人没什么特别。接下来十二个月里，会有大约二十三个人做一遍他今天要做的事。 他要能坐下开始干活，有四件事必须先成立。一个说明他是谁的账号。一台机器。一条能上网的路。还有这家公司干活要用的那一堆东西的席位。 这四件事，今天一件都不会建。每一件都必须在电梯门打开之前就已经成立。 星期一不建造任何东西。星期一只是把已经建好的东西显影出来。这才是这趟走读值得走的原因。 所以往回倒。某个地方的某个系统，判定了这个人存在。是哪一个？ 如果答案是"他主管提了个工单"，那就到此为止。这个答案下游的一切都会迟到、会不全，或者两样都占，而后面加多少自动化都补不回来。 真正值得问的那个问题更窄，也更难。哪个系统说了算：这个人还是不是这家公司的员工？ 必须有一个。不是两个大致吻合的，是一个，有名字的，别的所有系统都信它。 通常是 HR 在跑的那套，因为入职日和最后一天真正住在那里。它很少是大家希望的那个系统，而且几乎从来不是目录。 有了这个触发器，账号是简单的那一半。一个名字，一个邮箱，一个还没人用过的密码。 他能够到什么，是难的那一半，而它由一条规则决定——这条规则听起来像抠字眼，直到第二年。 一个组要么表示一个岗位职能，要么表示一束权限。绝不能两者都是。 因为一旦一个组同时是这两样，你就没法为了其中一个理由去改它而不动另一个。有人换了团队，他的权限就跟着一起动，无声地，朝着没人选过的方向。 而自动化是忠实的。它一字不差地执行你写下的模型。如果模型混淆了这两样，自动化就会以机器的速度把这份混淆传播到每一个新人身上，而且传得非常一致。 在这里，一致比零星更糟。零星的乱会被人注意到。一致的乱会变成"我们一直就是这么干的"。 这间办公室有八个职能。财务、销售、研发，再加另外五个。八是个小数目。小到没人觉得组模型值得专门设计一次，又大到设计错了要拆好几年。 同一周里的某一天，有人订了一台笔记本。 有意思的是它的镜像住在哪儿，而今天的答案是：不在这栋楼里。没有人在这里做镜像。厂商在发货之前就把这台机器登记到了这家公司名下，开机第一次联网，它自己去把策略拉下来。 这套东西替掉的是一台任务序列服务器、一个技术员，和每台机器三十到六十分钟。但它成立的前提是身份那部分先做对了。如果没有，这就不是零接触，这是一个套着零接触外衣的重装项目。 箱子本身周四到的，进了库房——就是那间带锁的屋子，紧挨着机柜。 库房不大。里面大概放五台备机、还没擦干净的退回机，以及在途的东西。五台听着很单薄，直到你算清楚它是干什么用的。 五台要盖住的是：下一批货到之前来报到的新人，大约每月两个；加上同一个月里坏掉的机器，不到一台。这是个交付周期的数，不是库存政策。 然后是席位。这间办公室能点得出名字的服务大约十个。一个目录、一个办公租户、文件存储、设备管理、终端安全、备份、远程访问、工单系统、会议，还有一个盯着上面这些的东西。 我们这位新人还需要至少一个不在这份名单上的席位，因为他team里有人一年半前刷卡买了它，而且没告诉过任何人。 记住这一句。它会在结尾回来，而且它是这趟走读里最贵的一句话。 回到电梯厅。八点五十。 从电梯到他工位的这段路会经过服务台，这不是巧合。服务台就在动线上，从开放区看得见，靠着它取件的库房，也靠着它作为第一响应人的机柜。 把同一个位置挪进后勤办公室，会发生一件很具体的事：走过来问的人变成了开工单的人。没有人决定要改变工作量。有人只是挪了一张桌子。 他的工位是七十张里的一张，在一层为"周二六十五个人"造的楼里。有把椅子，有块显示器，还有一台从来没开过机的机器。 第一次开机。它问他是谁。 注意它没问什么。它没问这台机器是什么，没问它在哪儿，没问它插在哪根线上。它问的是：拿着它的人是谁。 而当它接上网络，网络问的是同一个问题。那就是 802.1X，它背后是 RADIUS，RADIUS 背后是同一个签发了那个账号的目录。 端口什么都不决定。你可以把这台机器抱到这层楼的任何一张桌子上，或者拎进七间会议室里的任何一间，它落到的地方都一样。 落在员工段，因为他通过了认证。这层楼上有四个段，那一个是留给"证明了自己是谁"的人的。 另外三个是访客、打不了补丁的，和管理。 访客值得单说一句，因为它是唯一一个根本没有登记册的。你不会去给一位来访者做纳管。你按高峰日给这个段定容量，然后让它保持不受信任——而"刻意地不受信任"正是它安全的原因。 到午饭时候，我们这位新人已经在干活了。邮件、文件、聊天，还有他team赖以生存的那个工具。没有人带着他走过任何一个设置向导。 那么今天一共产生了几张工单？如果前面每一步都建对了，接近零。 这个数可以从两个方向逼近。支持模型说：零接触建成之后，装机与纳管每年产生大约五十三张工单。机队的算术说：这间办公室每年交接大约六十二台机器，换机周期和新人加在一起。 八次交接七张票。大部分机器换了手，没有任何人开任何单子；少数没换成。那个差额，就是一条能用的发放路径从外面看起来的样子。 这两个数是从完全不同的东西推出来的。一个从工单到达率，一个从换机周期。它们描述的是同一间办公室，而且对上了——这是这类规划唯一能拿到的那种确证。 现在把上面这一整套，做二十三遍。 再往反方向做大约十七遍，因为人会走。 这里是这趟走读脚下的地面发生变化的地方，值得说出来，而不是让它滑过去。 离职率那个数是借来的。中位十几这个带，是专业服务和科技行业的雇主通常所在的区间，而这个带来自公开的雇主统计，不是来自这里有谁真的管过这家公司的薪资册。 不是借来的，是结构。入职等于离职加净增。这句话是算术，它不在乎离职率是多少。 所以你尽管去动那个带。把它降到十分之一，这句话之后的每一个数都会变。而论证的形状一点都不会动——形状才是你能带回自己那栋楼里的东西。 取这个带的中位，一年下来大约四十次入职与离职事件。差不多每六个工作日一次。 不是一个项目。不是一个旺季。每六个工作日一次，租约跑多久就跑多久。 租约是五年。 这五年里，这间办公室会招进大约一百一十六个人。 为了净增三十个。 加上第一天就在这儿的那一百个，大约有两百一十六个不同的人，在某个时刻持有过这家公司的账号。 而这层楼，同一时刻最多装得下一百三十个。 这意味着目录不是办公室。它大约是办公室的一点七倍，而且这个比例只会往上走。 办公室是一张快照。登记册是一段历史。IT 管的每一个估算面都是后者，而所有人关于"规模"的直觉都是前者。 机器干的是一模一样的事。整个租约期买进大约两百二十台，为的是同时持有一百一十五台。 现在往前走三年，回去找星期一早上那个人。 他还在。一年半前他换了团队。 想一想三种生命周期事件各自给了你什么可抓的东西。入职有一个入职日。 离职有一个最后一天。 转岗有一次谈话。 没有事件触发。没有东西落进任何队列。不存在某一天有人被要求去看一眼，于是这次转岗就按"谈话"的方式被处理了——也就是，把现在需要的权限加上去。 然后不把不需要的拿掉。所有人都是这么建的。它看上去是完整的，因为入职跑得通，离职也跑得通。 两年和几次内部调动之后，在这儿待得最久的那些人，拥有全公司最多的权限，而他们没有一个说得清为什么。 没有人马虎。每一次单独的授权，在授出的那天都是正确的。失败之处在于：那条没有触发器的腿，始终没有被装上一个。 这是这间办公室里第一件永远没人触发的事。第二件在这里，而且更大。 数一数这栋楼里不是人的身份。大约有四十个。 其中二十六个是设备凭据，因为网络对所有东西都做认证，而门禁控制器、打印机、房间系统和电话亭设备都得自己回答"我是谁"。大约十二个是那十个有名字的服务之间的集成。还有两个是 break-glass 账号。 这间办公室每五个身份里，有两个不是人。 这四十个里，没有一个有入职日。 没有一个有主管。 也没有一个有最后一天。 想想那台门禁控制器。一次离职会强制审查一个人的权限，因为一个日期到了，一个流程启动了。而没有任何东西会强制审查一台门禁控制器的凭据。它是装修期间签发的，租约到期那天它还会在那儿。 那三个特权管理员账号是反证。它们最终确实会失效——因为它们背后的人，最终会离职。 现在前面那句话回来了。有人刷卡买的那个工具。 等我们这位新人有一天离职，离职流程会回收他在那十个叫得出名字的服务上的席位。它不会碰那一个，因为没有任何离职事件能到达一个没人写下来过的服务。 这不是一个"可以改进的回收率"。它不是百分之九十，也不是百分之八十。那里根本没有流程。 整个租约期里，八十六个人离开这家公司。对那十个之外的任何东西，没有人回收任何东西，因为负有回收义务的人不知道那个工具的存在。 有一个地方会让上面这一切显形，那就是工单队列。 把十六步要求的自动化都建起来。自助改密、零接触设备、自动化的入转离。它是有效的。它拿走了大约五分之二的工单量。 有一类纹丝不动。访问与权限。建完之后，它成了队列里最大的一块，超过三分之一。 这不是自动化的缺口。这是估算面在队列里现身了。 产生这些访问请求的，是一个五分之二不是人、且没有生命周期的身份人口，面对的是一个这家公司不知道有多大的服务估算面，中间隔着一本一年变一百二十三次的登记册。 把请求路径自动化，不会让上面任何一样东西变小。它只是让同样的请求来得更快。 看看十六步真正拿掉的是哪几类。改密。装机。入职和离职的批处理。每一类都是一个有确定答案的问题。 而活下来的那一类，结尾是一个人在判断：某个人该不该被允许拥有某样东西。这和 build-out 每一步在问"AI 能被信任到哪里"时，落到的是同一条边界。 下个星期一还会有一个。八点五十站在电梯厅里，没来过这里。 这层楼每个星期五清空，星期二再填满。六十五个人，空气里一百四十五个设备，七十张桌子，到周五下午只剩三成多一点，几乎没人。 估算面不会清空。在这份租约的整个生命里，它没有任何一天比前一天更小过。 所以当你在算一间百人办公室需要什么的时候，把人数一遍。一遍是为了桌子、天线和房间，那是这栋楼要问的。另一遍是为了每一个曾经持有过账号的人——那才是你实际在管的东西。

walkthrough/03-the-day-it-breaks.en.md.t: Walkthrough 03 · The day it breaks — the first ten minutes, and why the order matters
walkthrough/03-the-day-it-breaks.en.md.b: Walkthrough 03 · The day it breaks — the first ten minutes, and why the order matters It is twelve minutes past nine on a Tuesday. Tuesday is the busy day here. About sixty-five of the hundred people on payroll are in the building, which is most of the people this floor ever holds at once. Somebody walks up to the service desk. They can do that without deciding to, because the desk sits on the walk from the lift to the seats, which is a choice somebody made on a plan, two walks back. What they say is one sentence. I cannot get in. It just says it cannot sign me in. Ninety seconds later a second person says the same sentence. Not a similar one. The same one. That is worth being careful about, because it is tempting to hear two reports and think you have two pieces of information. You have one piece of information, said twice. And the sentence carries almost nothing. It tells you somebody tried and something refused, and it does not tell you which of the things in the chain refused, or whether the same thing refused both times. Here is why that matters. Take remote access, the one place in this office where this exact sentence shows up most. Four completely unrelated faults produce it. A certificate on the gateway that expired over the weekend. An identity provider having a bad hour. A captive portal on a hotel network, intercepting. And a tunnel that installs a more specific route which does not happen to carry the traffic authentication uses. Four different incidents. Four different fixes. One report, word for word identical in all four. From where you are standing at the desk, the symptom is carrying zero diagnostic information. So the first question is not what is broken. The first question is what exactly is it. There is a rung below the first rung, and it costs nothing, and it is the one people skip. Three things, established and written down somewhere the ticket can see them. The exact name or the exact address. Not the site. The name. From which machine. Not from a person. From a machine, in a place, on a network. And what working would look like. What would you see, if this were fine. If you cannot state that third one, you are not debugging. You are sympathising. The reason this rung exists is dull and it is real. The thing the user calls the site has four names. Two of them are aliases. One of them resolves to something different inside this building than it does outside it. The most expensive hour in this job is the one spent climbing the whole ladder correctly, against the wrong target. While that is being written down, look up. The floor is fine. The doors open. The lights are on. The lift works. Somebody is making coffee. And the room the first walkthrough took you into is fine too. Three access switches, a core, six radios in the ceiling, a controller. All of it up. Nothing on this floor is broken. That is not a relief. That is the shape of the problem. A decade ago a dead circuit meant no email and no internet, and the file server and the domain controller kept working in the next room. People were annoyed. People were not stopped. Today a dead circuit means nobody can log in. For an office whose work lives entirely off site, the uplink is the business. There is a question this office already asked itself, in a calmer moment, when it was deciding what deserved a place in that room. What has to keep working here on a day the uplink is down. The honest list is short. Getting into the building. Getting out of it. And the fire panel. Everybody's work is in a tenant they cannot reach anyway. A company like this one does not need local continuity for its work. It needs it for its doors. That is a much smaller requirement than most arguments for keeping a server room assume. Now, before anybody touches anything, there is a decision. It is the most consequential thing that happens in the first ten minutes and it is not a technical decision. Do you stop the bleeding first, or do you find out what is bleeding. Every version of this advice you have ever heard says mitigate first. Roll it back, fail it over, turn the thing off, put people on the other path. Then investigate. The slogan is right. It is also not unconditional, and the difference between knowing the slogan and knowing its conditions is most of what seniority is on this particular subject. Measured against a realistic spread of causes, mitigating first saves about nine minutes of mean downtime. That is the win, and it is a real one. It also costs about six minutes in the tail. The worst case gets worse. And the six is not mysterious. It is exactly the mitigation window. Six minutes spent attempting a generic fix on a cause that generic fix was never going to cover. Which means the incident that costs you the extra six minutes is, by definition, one of the ones the mitigation could not help. The worst incident you will ever have is one of those. That trade is the right way round. You take a small, bounded, known cost on the rare incident in order to remove a large one from every common incident. Anybody who quotes you the nine minutes and not the six is selling. And it inverts. If the generic mitigation covers less than about forty percent of the plausible causes, diagnosing first is the better call. The advice is not a law. It is a bet on your own coverage. There is a second condition, and it is the one that catches people. Some mitigations can make things worse. A failover that flaps. A rollback that corrupts. A restart that loses the queue. Once the expected damage from attempting the mitigation gets past about ten minutes, mitigating first is simply the wrong call. So the thing worth being able to say out loud is not the slogan. It is the two conditions under which the slogan stops being true. And notice what that means about the rehearsed failover and the tested restore elsewhere in this building. They are not insurance against the incident. They are what makes this instinct correct in the first place. Mitigation is running. Now you climb. Does the name resolve, and to what you think. Is there a route, and does the return path exist. Do the filters allow it, both layers, both directions. Do small packets work and big ones hang. And only then, may you look. Each rung is cheaper than the one below it and eliminates more than the one below it. That is the entire design, and it is why skipping is expensive rather than untidy. And there is one rule that decides whether something is a rung at all. A check earns its place by what it eliminates, not by what it reports. Restart the client eliminates nothing. All four of those causes are still possible afterwards. Is the tunnel connected eliminates nothing either. Same four, still standing. They feel like progress because they produce a result. Producing a result and removing a possibility are different things, and only one of them is debugging. This is also why one very famous command has no rung of its own. A ping that fails is consistent with a routing problem, a filter, a dead host, and a policy that simply drops it. It eliminates nothing. Which is not an argument against running it. It is an argument against believing it. One rung carries the highest information answer in this whole business, and the answer is a single word. Refused means your packet arrived, and something at the far end actively said no. Routing works. Filtering to that host works. The problem is at the other end, and it is a service not listening or bound to the wrong interface. You just eliminated three rungs with one word. Timed out means you know nothing. A dropped packet, a black holing filter, a wrong route and a dead host all look exactly like this, and there is no way to tell them apart from here. A timeout is not an answer. It is the ladder telling you to keep climbing. There is one rung people skip and then spend the rest of the day underneath. The signature is unmistakable once you have seen it. The handshake completes and the transfer stalls. Logging in works. Downloading does not. And a failure here tells you more than a fix would. The packet size where it breaks names the overhead, and the overhead names the encapsulation. The thing that is wrong announces which tunnel it is wearing. And now, four rungs later, you may open a capture. Not before. You arrive at the capture with a hypothesis, because four rungs eliminated the alternatives, and you open it to confirm or kill that hypothesis and then you stop. A capture opened without a hypothesis is a hobby. Go back to the four causes and the one sentence, and watch what the difference actually buys. Checks chosen for what they rule out resolve all four. Every time. With a bounded worst case. Habit resolves two of the four. On the other two it spends the same number of checks and finishes unable to say which one it is. And there is a trap in the middle of it. Asking whether you can reach the identity provider returns exactly the same answer whether the provider is genuinely down or a hotel captive portal is intercepting you. The check cannot tell those two apart. The one observation that does separate them is whether a name you already know resolves to the answer you already know. And the fourth cause fails after the word connected. The tunnel reports connected. Authentication still fails. Every check that asks whether it is up answers yes. Which makes the reflex check worse than useless on that one. It does not merely fail to help. It points away from the fault. Everything up to this point is ground the person telling you this has stood on. Ladders, tunnels, names that resolve differently indoors, the day the certificate expires over a weekend. What comes next is different footing, and it is worth saying so out loud rather than letting the voice stay level. The next part is the process around the outage, and it is mapped and verified rather than lived at scale. So. How many people are handling this. There is one walk-up service desk position on this floor. One. It sits on the circulation route, beside the store it draws spares from and beside the rack it is first responder for. The support window is eight in the morning to six in the evening, Monday to Friday. That is fifty hours against a forty hour week, and it is the number that actually decides staffing, which is why it gets written down as a choice rather than absorbed as an assumption. And after the automation this office is supposed to build, the queue runs at about forty-eight tickets a week. When something like this morning happens, the instinct is to add people to it. Responders do not add up linearly. Every one of them has to be told what is already known, and the telling comes out of the same minutes as the fixing. Model that and the curve flattens fast. Adding responders stops paying at about five. This office does not have five. It has one position and whoever else can be pulled off what they were doing. Which means incident commander here is not a role. It is a hat, and this morning it is probably on the same head as everything else. The point of the role was never the ceremony. It is that somebody is deciding and somebody is recording. When it is one tired person, they are doing both, and knowing that is what stops the response from becoming a scramble that nobody can reconstruct afterwards. There is one failure mode worth naming because it is invisible from inside. Heads down, fixing, no updates. Leadership panics, piles on, and now the responder is answering questions instead of working. Still working, next update in fifteen. That sentence costs nothing and it buys the next fifteen minutes. And the record is not admin. A post-mortem is only ever as good as what somebody wrote down while it was happening, and nobody has ever reconstructed a timeline accurately from memory the following afternoon. While that is going on, there is something else true about this floor that nobody is looking at. About twenty-six things on it will never tell you anything useful. Door controllers. Printers. The room systems. The booth devices. Vendor firmware, on the vendor's schedule, and no way to change either. You can see whether they answer. You cannot see what they are doing. And no purchase changes that, which is the part worth sitting with. The first limit on monitoring is not your tooling. It is the other end. The second limit is worse, because it is invisible. You can only monitor what you know about. Coverage is always measured against an inventory. If the inventory is a subset of what exists, then the coverage percentage is a statement about the subset, and it is a true statement, and it is answering a smaller question than the one you asked. It will read as ninety-eight percent while the thing that broke this morning sits outside it. Third. Every monitored thing costs a credential. An agent needs an identity, and that identity has no start date, no manager and no last day. At full coverage, the monitoring platform is the most privileged system in this building, and almost nobody designs it as though it were. And fourth, coverage is not detection. You can collect everything and detect nothing. An alert nobody acts on is a dashboard. So replace the objective. Monitor everything cannot be achieved, and more usefully, it cannot be checked. There is no test that tells you that you got there. Knowing what you are not monitoring can be both. It turns coverage from an aspiration into a subtraction. This is the estate you can enumerate. This is the part of it that reports. And this list in between is where an incident will be slower, deliberately, and here is the reason for each line. That list is the deliverable. It is also the only thing in this section that survives a change of tooling. At some point this morning, it comes back. Somebody renews something, or a provider's status page goes green, and the floor stops looking up. The fix is not the deliverable. Every incident's real deliverable is the gap it exposed, closed. The log line nobody was writing. The service nobody had instrumented. The alert that would have fired before anybody walked up to that desk. And the review is blameless, which is not a kindness and not a culture slogan. Blame makes people leave things out. Things left out make the next one worse. It is an operational requirement wearing a nice word. There is one more thing to look at before the floor goes quiet, and it is the same limit as the monitoring one, arriving from the other side. Company information in this office lives in five places. The tenant. The endpoints. The directory. The records the IT function keeps about itself. And the services nobody listed. Four of those five can be given a recovery objective. The fifth cannot, and the reason is not budget or effort. You cannot set a recovery objective for a system you have not inventoried. Which is the monitoring limit again, in different clothes. Both of them stop at the edge of the same list, and neither of them tells you where the edge is. Two of the most expensive guarantees this function makes, and they fail at the same place. This office performs one restore drill a year, and records that it did. That drill is not paperwork. It is the only place in this entire building where we can recover stops being an opinion and becomes a thing somebody watched happen, on a date, with a duration attached. It is the afternoon now. The floor is full again. Sixty-five people, a hundred and forty-five devices in the air, seventy desks and somebody in a booth. In a month nobody in this building will remember how long this morning took. What will still be true is which rung got skipped, and whether anybody wrote down why. The first walk counted the radios. The second counted the people twice, once for the desks and once for everyone who has ever held an account. This one counts the minutes. And the only minutes worth defending are the ones somebody spent because they decided to. Every other minute this morning was spent because nobody had decided anything, and those are the ones that come back.

walkthrough/03-the-day-it-breaks.zh.md.t: 走读 03 · 它坏掉的那一天——头十分钟，以及顺序为什么要紧
walkthrough/03-the-day-it-breaks.zh.md.b: 走读 03 · 它坏掉的那一天——头十分钟，以及顺序为什么要紧 星期二，上午九点十二分。星期二是这里最满的一天。一百个在册的人里，大约六十五个在楼里，这差不多就是这层楼同时装过的最多人数。 有人走到了服务台。他不用特意决定要来，因为这张台子就在从电梯走到工位的那条路上——那是两次走读之前，某个人在图纸上做的选择。 他说的是一句话。我进不去。它只说没法给我登录。 九十秒后，第二个人说了同一句话。不是类似的一句。是同一句。 这件事值得小心，因为听见两个人报障，很容易以为自己拿到了两条信息。你拿到的是一条信息，被说了两遍。 而这句话几乎什么都没带。它告诉你有人试了、有东西拒绝了，它没告诉你这条链上是哪一样拒绝的，也没告诉你两次拒绝的是不是同一样。 为什么这要紧。拿远程访问来说，这句话在这间办公室里出现得最多的地方就是它。四个毫不相干的故障都会产出这句话。网关上一张周末过期的证书。身份提供方过了糟糕的一小时。酒店网络上一个正在拦截的 captive portal。以及一条隧道装了一条更具体的路由，而那条路由恰好不承载认证要走的流量。 四次不同的故障。四个不同的修法。一句报障，四次里一字不差。站在服务台这个位置上，这个症状携带的诊断信息是零。 所以第一个问题不是"什么坏了"。 第一个问题是，"它"到底是什么。 第一级之下还有一级，它不花钱，而它正是人们会跳过的那一级。三件事，问清楚，并且写在工单看得见的地方。 准确的那个名字，或者准确的那个地址。不是"那个站点"。是名字。 从哪台机器上。不是从哪个人。是从一台机器，在一个地方，接在一个网络上。 以及，"好了"应该是什么样。如果它是正常的，你会看到什么。 如果第三条你说不出来，那你不是在排障。你是在共情。 这一级之所以存在，理由既枯燥又真实。用户嘴里那个"站点"有四个名字。其中两个是别名。还有一个，在这栋楼里面解析出来的结果，和在外面不一样。 这份工作里最贵的一个小时，是把整架梯子完全正确地爬了一遍——爬在错的目标上。 趁着这些正在被写下来，抬头看一眼。 这层楼没事。门能开。灯亮着。电梯在跑。有人在煮咖啡。 第一次走读带你进过的那个房间也没事。三台接入交换机、一台核心、天花板上六个射频、一台控制器。全都在。 这层楼上没有任何东西坏了。这不是一件让人松口气的事。这就是问题的形状。 十来年前，线路断了意味着没有邮件、没有互联网，而文件服务器和域控还在隔壁房间照常跑着。人会烦。人不会停。 今天，线路断了意味着没有人能登录。对一间工作完全在场外的办公室来说，那条上行链路就是这门生意本身。 这间办公室在更冷静的时候已经问过自己一个问题——当时它在决定，那个房间里什么东西配留下。上行断掉的那一天，这里有什么必须继续工作。 诚实的清单很短。进得了这栋楼。出得了这栋楼。还有消防盘。 所有人的工作都在一个他们本来就够不着的租户里。像这样一间公司，不需要为它的工作准备本地续命能力。它需要的是为它的门准备。这个要求，比大多数"保留一个机房"的论证所假设的，要小得多。 现在，在有人动手之前，有一个决定。它是头十分钟里后果最重的那件事，而它不是一个技术决定。 你是先止血，还是先弄清楚在流什么血。 你听过的每一个版本都说：先缓解。回滚、切换、把那东西关掉、把人放到另一条路上。然后再查。 这句口号是对的。它同时也不是无条件的。而在这个问题上，知道这句口号和知道它的条件之间的差距，几乎就是"资深"的全部含义。 拿一个现实的成因分布去量，先缓解平均省下大约九分钟的停摆时间。这是那份收益，而且是真的。 它同时在尾部付出大约六分钟。最坏的情况变得更坏了。 而那六分钟一点都不神秘。它恰好就是那个缓解窗口。六分钟花在对一个成因做通用修复上，而那个通用修复本来就覆盖不到它。 也就是说，让你多付六分钟的那次故障，按定义就是缓解帮不上忙的那一类。而你这辈子最糟的那次故障，就是其中一次。 这笔交易的方向是对的。你在罕见的那次故障上，承担一份小的、有界的、已知的代价，换掉每一次常见故障上的一份大代价。谁只跟你报那九分钟、不报那六分钟，谁就是在推销。 而且它会翻转。如果那个通用缓解覆盖不到大约四成的可能成因，那先诊断才是更好的选择。这条建议不是定律。它是一场押在你自己覆盖率上的赌。 还有第二个条件，而这个是真正会绊倒人的。有些缓解手段会把事情弄得更糟。一次来回抖动的切换。一次会损坏数据的回滚。一次把队列丢掉的重启。一旦"尝试这个缓解"的期望损失超过大约十分钟，先缓解就干脆是错的。 所以值得说出口的，不是那句口号。是那两个让口号不再成立的条件。而且请注意这对这栋楼里别处那些演练过的切换、测试过的恢复意味着什么。它们不是给故障买的保险。它们是让这个直觉一开始就成立的原因。 缓解在跑了。现在开始爬。 这个名字解不解析得出来，解析成的是不是你以为的那个。有没有路由，回程路径在不在。过滤放不放行，两层都要，两个方向都要。小包能过而大包会卡吗。然后，也只有到那时，你才可以去看。 每一级都比它下面那一级更便宜，而且比下面那一级排除得更多。这就是这架梯子设计的全部，也是为什么跳级是"贵"，而不只是"不整齐"。 有一条规则决定一样东西算不算得上是一级。一个检查凭它排除了什么赢得位置，不是凭它报告了什么。 重启客户端什么都排除不掉。那四个成因，做完之后一个不少。 隧道连上了吗，同样什么都排除不掉。还是那四个，全都站着。 它们让人觉得有进展，是因为它们产出了一个结果。产出一个结果和去掉一种可能，是两回事，而只有其中一件叫排障。 这也是为什么有一条非常有名的命令，在这架梯子上没有自己的一级。 一次失败的 ping，和路由问题、和过滤、和主机已死、和一条单纯丢弃它的策略，全都相容。它什么都排除不掉。这不是反对你去跑它。这是反对你去信它。 有一级承载着这整门手艺里信息量最高的那个回答，而那个回答只有一个词。 拒绝，意味着你的包到了，而对面主动说了不。路由是通的。到那台主机的过滤是通的。问题在另一端，是一个没在监听、或者绑错了网卡的服务。你刚刚用一个词排除掉了三级。 超时，意味着你什么都不知道。一个被丢掉的包、一条黑洞式的过滤、一条错的路由、一台死掉的主机，从这里看过去长得一模一样，你分不出来。 超时不是一个答案。它是梯子在告诉你，接着往上爬。 有一级是人们会跳过、然后在它下面耗掉一整天的。 它的特征你见过一次就再也认得出来。握手完成了，传输卡住了。登录成功。下载不动。 而这一级失败给你的信息，比一个修复给你的还多。它断在哪个包长，那个包长就说出了开销；那份开销就说出了封装。坏掉的那样东西，会自己报出它披的是哪条隧道。 现在，四级之后，你可以打开抓包了。 不能更早。你带着一个假设来到抓包这一步，因为四级已经把别的可能排除掉了；你打开它是为了确认或者杀死这个假设，然后就停。没有假设就打开的抓包，是一项爱好。 回到那四个成因和那一句话，看看这个差别到底买到了什么。 按"能排除什么"挑出来的检查，四个全部解得开。每一次都解得开。而且最坏情况有界。 凭习惯来，四个里解开两个。另外两个，它花掉同样多的检查次数，最后说不出是哪一个。 而中间还埋着一个陷阱。问"我够得到身份提供方吗"，在提供方真的挂了、和一个酒店 captive portal 正在拦你这两种情况下，返回的是完全一样的答案。这个检查分不开它们。 唯一能把它们分开的那个观察，是你早就知道的一个名字，解析出来的是不是你早就知道的那个答案。 而第四个成因，是在"已连接"这个词之后才失败的。隧道报告已连接。认证照样失败。 每一个问"它在不在"的检查都回答"在"。这让那个反射式检查在这一个成因上比没用还糟。它不只是帮不上忙。它把你指向了远离故障的方向。 到这里为止的一切，都是讲这些话的人自己站过的地面。梯子、隧道、在楼里楼外解析得不一样的名字、证书在周末过期的那一天。接下来这一段是不同的地面，而这一点值得说出口，而不是让声音保持一样平。接下来讲的是围着故障的那套流程，它是测绘过、验证过的，不是在规模上活过的。 那么。有多少人在处理这件事。 这层楼上有一个走读式服务台席位。一个。它在动线上，挨着它取备件的库房，挨着它作为第一响应人的那个机柜。 支持窗口是早八点到晚六点，周一到周五。那是五十小时，对着一周四十小时的工时，而它才是真正决定人员配置的那个数字——所以它被当成一个选择写下来，而不是被当成一个假设吸收掉。 而在这间办公室该建的那套自动化建成之后，队列跑在每周大约四十八张工单上。 今天早上这种事发生的时候，本能反应是往上加人。 响应者不是线性叠加的。每多一个，都得有人把"目前已知什么"讲给他，而讲这件事的时间，和修这件事的时间是同一批分钟。把这一点建进模型，曲线很快就平了。加人到大约第五个，就不再划算。 这间办公室没有五个。它有一个席位，加上任何一个能被从手头活里拉过来的人。 也就是说，这里的"事故指挥官"不是一个角色。它是一顶帽子，而今天早上，它多半戴在那个已经戴着所有别的帽子的脑袋上。 这个角色的意义从来不是那套仪式。它的意义是：有人在做决定，有人在做记录。当这两件事落在同一个疲惫的人身上时，知道自己在同时做这两件事，就是让响应不至于变成一场事后没人能重建的乱局的那个东西。 有一种失败模式值得点名，因为从里面看不见。埋头修，不出声。管理层慌了，涌上来，于是响应者开始回答问题而不是干活。还在处理，十五分钟后再更新一次。这句话不花钱，而它买下了接下来的十五分钟。 而那份记录不是行政工作。一份复盘的质量上限，就是当时有人写下来的那些东西；从来没有人能在第二天下午凭记忆准确重建一条时间线。 在这些事情进行的同时，这层楼上还有一件没人在看的事，也是真的。 它上面大约有二十六样东西，永远不会告诉你任何有用的东西。 门禁控制器。打印机。会议室系统。电话亭设备。厂商的固件，走厂商的日程，两样你都改不了。 你能看见它们答不答。你看不见它们在做什么。而且没有哪笔采购能改变这件事——这才是值得坐下来想想的那部分。监控的第一道限制不在你的工具。它在对面那一端。 第二道限制更糟，因为它看不见。你只能监控你知道存在的东西。 覆盖率永远是对着一份清册量出来的。如果那份清册是实际存在之物的一个子集，那这个覆盖率百分比就是一句关于这个子集的陈述，而且是一句真话，而且它回答的是一个比你所问的更小的问题。 它会读作百分之九十八，而今天早上坏掉的那样东西就坐在它外面。 第三。每一个被监控的东西都要花掉一份凭据。一个 agent 需要一个身份，而那个身份没有入职日期、没有主管、也没有最后一天。在全覆盖之下，那套监控平台是这栋楼里权限最高的系统，而几乎没有人把它当成那样来设计。 第四，覆盖不是检测。你可以收集一切，然后什么都检测不到。一条没人去动的告警，就是一块仪表盘。 所以把目标换掉。"监控一切"做不到，而且更有用的是，它没法核查。没有任何一项检验能告诉你，你到了。 "知道你没在监控什么"，这两件事它都做得到。它把覆盖率从一个愿景变成一次减法。这是你数得出来的那片估算面。这是它里面会报数的那部分。而中间这份清单，就是故障会变慢的那一块，是刻意的，而且每一行都有它的理由。 那份清单才是交付物。它也是这一段里唯一一件熬得过工具更替的东西。 今天上午的某个时刻，它回来了。有人续了什么，或者某个厂商的状态页转绿了，然后这层楼就不再抬头看了。 修好它，不是交付物。 每一次故障真正的交付物，是它暴露出来的那个缺口，被补上。那行没人在写的日志。那个没人埋过点的服务。那条本该在任何人走到服务台之前就响的告警。 而那场复盘是不追责的——这不是一种体贴，也不是一句文化口号。追责会让人把事情漏掉不说。被漏掉的事情会让下一次更糟。它是一条运维上的硬要求，穿了一个好听的词。 在这层楼安静下来之前，还有一样东西值得看，而它就是刚才那道监控限制，从另一侧走过来。 这间办公室的公司信息住在五个地方。那个租户。那些终端。那个目录。IT 自己关于自己保存的记录。以及那些没人列出来过的服务。 这五个里有四个能被赋予一个恢复目标。第五个不能，而理由不是预算也不是力气。你没法为一个你没有盘点过的系统设定恢复目标。 这就是刚才那道监控限制，换了身衣服。两者都停在同一份清单的边缘上，而两者都不会告诉你那条边缘在哪。这个职能做出的两项最昂贵的保证，坏在同一个地方。 这间办公室一年做一次恢复演练，并且把"做过了"记下来。 那次演练不是文书工作。它是这整栋楼里唯一一个地方，让"我们恢复得了"不再是一个意见，而变成一件有人看着它发生过、有日期、还带着一个时长的事。 现在是下午了。这层楼又满了。六十五个人，空中一百四十五台设备，七十张桌子，还有人在电话亭里。 一个月之后，这栋楼里没有人会记得今天上午花了多久。 仍然为真的，是哪一级被跳过了，以及有没有人把跳过它的理由写下来。 第一次走读数的是射频。第二次把人数了两遍，一遍为了桌子，一遍为了所有曾经持有过账号的人。这一次数的是分钟。 而唯一值得辩护的那些分钟，是有人因为做了决定才花掉的。今天上午其余的每一分钟，都是因为没有人做过任何决定才花掉的——而回来找你的，正是那些。

walkthrough/README.md.b: The Walkthrough — the reference office, told out loud > A route through the other axes, like build-out/ and for > the same reason: it teaches no page this repo does not already hold. What it adds is an > order and a register — one hundred-person office, walked through slowly, in a > voice the rest of this repo deliberately does not use. > Decision: docs/adr/0009 Written to be spoken by a text-to-speech engine and heard — never read. That is not a style note. It decides the whole format: no tables, no inline links, no as the table above shows , no parenthetical asides, and numbers written the way a person says them. A walkthrough/ .md contains the words that get spoken and nothing else. What comes out of one script No audio is committed here. You generate it with your own credentials, or you listen to the published episode. A recording in the tree would serve one voice, one language and one speaking rate, and would be wrong for everyone else. Three artifacts, and each one has to stand alone Because three audiences each lack a different thing, and the third is the one that decides the most: · Audience · Has · Lacks · · A reader on GitHub · the script · the picture, the sound · · A reader in site/ · the script, the floor · the sound, unless they wire up TTS · · A listener on a podcast · the sound · any screen at all · The last row is why the honesty markers are spoken . A 🔨 or 🧭 badge drawn on the floor does not exist for a listener, so the narrator says the boundary out loud, in the story's own voice, at the moment the footing changes. In the first walkthrough it changes once — from the segmentation and addressing material the author has run, to the wireless arithmetic the-reference-office.md already flags as drawn from published vendor guidance rather than from having lived with a deployment. Beats One beat is one paragraph, one TTS call, one audio segment, one floor state. It is delimited by an HTML comment carrying a stable id, which GitHub, the viewer and the speech engine all ignore: markdown The id is a name, never a number. Insert a paragraph into a hundred-and-forty-beat script and every ordinal after it shifts — silently, because a floor pointing at the wrong beat looks exactly like a floor pointing at the right one. Alignment is by beat and never by timestamp, so any engine, any voice and any language works without configuring anything: see docs/adr/0012 . Two languages, and neither is a translation .en.md and .zh.md sit side by side here, not under docs/zh/ . That directory means mirror , and these are not mirrors: translation preserves facts and destroys cadence, which is the one thing a spoken script is made of. Each script is canonical for its own cadence. Both declare the same sources: , and a disagreement between them is settled by reading the source both are accountable to — never by preferring one script over the other. The repo-wide rule that English is the source of truth is unchanged everywhere else; here it has been narrowed to the job it was always doing, which is arbitrating facts . The reasoning is in docs/adr/0010 . The floor The viewer renders an interactive 2D office the walkthrough plays over — pan, zoom, clickable props, and a cast of figures who are the wireless load rather than decoration. Zoom is semantic in three registers: occupancy and coverage far out, placement in the middle, and the path from access port to uplink close in. The buttons name their subject as well as their scale: Floor frames the whole plate, Rack frames the IDF, and Room keeps the enclosure already in view (or the enclosure holding the prop you just clicked). With no current enclosure, Room opens the large meeting room. Choosing a register or occupancy day keeps that browsing choice through a window resize; Back , Next and Play return control to the walkthrough beat. It is a view . It renders numbers the Markdown states and computes none of its own, and a prop's panel shows the judgement and the criteria — never a device configuration, which this repo does not hold. The line, and what it costs to hold it, is docs/adr/0011 . The scene data lives beside the scripts, not under site/ , because a fact the viewer holds alone is a fact lost the moment the viewer is deleted. It comes in two halves: · The plate — reference-office.plate.json · What this floor is : the spaces, what each is next to, and how you walk between them. Shared by every walkthrough, because walkthrough two is the same office. · · The walkthrough — .floor.json · What this walkthrough says about it : the prop panels and the beat cues. In walkthrough one those panels are five times the size of the geometry, and every word of them is about networking. · The plate stops at topology — no corridor widths, no egress distances, no sanitary provision, no claim it would pass anything (ADR-0014). What it does claim is checked: a headless Godot project walks the floor from the lift lobby along circulation and reports anything it cannot reach. It caught two doors opening onto nothing the first time it ran. Generating the audio yourself Each beat is one call. Split on the beat comments, send each paragraph to whatever engine you have, and play the segments in order — the floor advances on each segment ending and needs no timing data. Nothing in this repo depends on which engine you pick. Adding a walkthrough 1. Pick what it is about, not which step it is. The sequence here is its own: the first walkthrough spans three documents across two axes plus the root. This is not build-out/ with a voice on top and the numbers do not correspond. 2. List the sources: first. Every fact spoken must be traceable to one of them. If a sentence needs a fact no source holds, the fact gets written into the material first — the walkthrough is never where something first appears. 3. Write beats, name them, and keep the file speakable. Read it aloud once before generating anything; the places you run out of breath are the places to split. 4. Write the second language as its own script , not as a translation of the first. 5. Freeze on publication. Record published: and the source fingerprints. After that the script is not edited — an error becomes an erratum in the document, because the recording cannot be amended and a silent fix would leave it lying. The footing changes once, out loud, where the 🔨 segmentation and addressing material gives way to the 🧭 wireless arithmetic. Walkthrough 02 is 93 beats , and it draws on the-reference-office.md , build-out/03-identity.md , build-out/04-devices-and-images.md and build-out/15-joiner-mover-leaver.md . It plays over the same plate — episode two is the same office — and everything that differs is in its panels, which are about identity and lifecycle where 01's were about the network. Its footing changes once, out loud, at the turnover band. Walkthrough 03 is 102 beats , and it draws on the-reference-office.md , build-out/01-uplink.md , debug-ladder.md , incident-response.md , the-stack/06-observability.md and the READMEs of the four-causes and mitigate-before-diagnose labs — seven sources, the most of any so far, because an incident is where the axes meet. Same plate again. Three of its ten props are plans rather than places : the decision, the ladder and the record are what this walkthrough is about and none of them has a location on a floor. Its footing changes once, out loud, where the 🔨 ladder gives way to the 🧭 incident-command process. One floor, three ways to see it. 01 reads the plate, 02 reads the estate standing on it, and 03 reads the clock. That is why the two things 03 spends longest on are the two this office cannot buy its way out of: what a check eliminates, and where the inventory ends — the monitoring limit and the recovery limit turn out to be the same limit approached from either side. Further walkthroughs are written when there is something worth saying out loud, one at a time, the way toolbox/ grows. There is no target count. Checking one bash python3 walkthrough/guard-walkthrough.py # beats, anchors, format, freeze python3 tools/floor/build-tiles.py --check # the floor's sprite sheet python3 tools/floor/prove-topology.py --check # is the plate still proved? Nothing here is generated — the script is the TTS input, so there is no derived artifact to fall behind. What the checker guards is that the two languages carry the same beats in the same order, that the floor cues only beats that exist, that every prop anchor is a real heading in a real file, and that the spoken text holds nothing a speech engine would read as noise or drop in silence. --freeze stamps published: and a fingerprint of each source. After that a changed source is reported as the recording now describes a document that moved , which is the signal to re-record — and the script itself is no longer edited.
